{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''invariant measure''' is a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] that is preserved by some [[Function (mathematics)|function]]. The function may be a [[geometric transformation]]. For examples, [[angle|circular angle]] is invariant under rotation, [[hyperbolic angle]] is  invariant under [[squeeze mapping]], and a difference of [[slope]]s is invariant under [[shear mapping]].<ref>{{wikibooks-inline|Geometry/Unified Angles}}</ref>

[[Ergodic theory]] is the study of invariant measures in [[dynamical systems]]. The [[Krylov–Bogolyubov theorem]] proves the existence of invariant measures under certain conditions on the function and space under consideration.

==Definition==

Let <math>(X, \Sigma)</math> be a [[measurable space]] and let <math>f : X \to X</math> be a [[measurable function]] from <math>X</math> to itself. A measure <math>\mu</math> on <math>(X, \Sigma)</math> is said to be '''invariant under''' <math>f</math> if, for every measurable set <math>A</math> in <math>\Sigma,</math>
<math display=block>\mu\left(f^{-1}(A)\right) = \mu(A).</math>

In terms of the [[pushforward measure]], this states that <math>f_*(\mu) = \mu.</math>

The collection of measures (usually [[probability measure]]s) on <math>X</math> that are invariant under <math>f</math> is sometimes denoted <math>M_f(X).</math> The collection of [[Ergodic (adjective)|ergodic measures]], <math>E_f(X),</math> is a subset of <math>M_f(X).</math> Moreover, any [[convex combination]] of two invariant measures is also invariant, so <math>M_f(X)</math> is a [[convex set]]; <math>E_f(X)</math> consists precisely of the extreme points of <math>M_f(X).</math>

In the case of a [[Dynamical system (definition)|dynamical system]] <math>(X, T, \varphi),</math> where <math>(X, \Sigma)</math> is a measurable space as before, <math>T</math> is a [[monoid]] and <math>\varphi : T \times X \to X</math> is the flow map, a measure <math>\mu</math> on <math>(X, \Sigma)</math> is said to be an '''invariant measure''' if it is an invariant measure for each map <math>\varphi_t : X \to X.</math> Explicitly, <math>\mu</math> is invariant [[if and only if]]
<math display=block>\mu\left(\varphi_{t}^{-1}(A)\right) = \mu(A) \qquad \text{ for all }  t \in T, A \in \Sigma.</math>

Put another way, <math>\mu</math> is an invariant measure for a sequence of [[random variable]]s <math>\left(Z_t\right)_{t \geq 0}</math> (perhaps a [[Markov chain]] or the solution to a [[stochastic differential equation]]) if, whenever the initial condition <math>Z_0</math> is distributed according to <math>\mu,</math> so is <math>Z_t</math> for any later time <math>t.</math>

When the dynamical system can be described by a [[transfer operator]], then the invariant measure is an eigenvector of the operator, corresponding to an eigenvalue of <math>1,</math> this being the largest eigenvalue as given by the [[Frobenius–Perron theorem]].

==Examples==

[[File:Hyperbolic sector squeeze mapping.svg|250px|right|thumb|[[Squeeze mapping]] leaves [[hyperbolic angle]] invariant as it moves a [[hyperbolic sector]] (purple) to one of the same area. Blue and green rectangles also keep the same area]]
* Consider the [[real line]] <math>\R</math> with its usual [[Borel sigma algebra|Borel σ-algebra]]; fix <math>a \in \R</math> and consider the translation map <math>T_a : \R \to \R</math> given by: <math display=block>T_a(x) = x + a.</math> Then one-dimensional [[Lebesgue measure]] <math>\lambda</math> is an invariant measure for <math>T_a.</math>
* More generally, on <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^n</math> with its usual Borel σ-algebra, <math>n</math>-dimensional Lebesgue measure <math>\lambda^n</math> is an invariant measure for any [[isometry]] of Euclidean space, that is, a map <math>T : \R^n \to \R^n</math> that can be written as <math display=block>T(x) = A x + b</math> for some <math>n \times n</math> [[orthogonal matrix]] <math>A \in O(n)</math> and a vector <math>b \in \R^n.</math>
* The invariant measure in the first example is unique up to trivial renormalization with a constant factor. This does not have to be necessarily the case: Consider a set consisting of just two points <math>\mathbf{S} = \{A,B\}</math> and the identity map <math>T = \operatorname{Id}</math> which leaves each point fixed. Then any probability measure <math>\mu : \mathbf{S} \to \R</math> is invariant. Note that <math>\mathbf{S}</math> trivially has a decomposition into <math>T</math>-invariant components <math>\{A\}</math> and <math>\{B\}.</math>
* [[Area]] measure in the Euclidean plane is invariant under the [[special linear group]] <math>\operatorname{SL}(2, \R)</math> of the <math>2 \times 2</math> [[Real matrix|real matrices]] of [[determinant]] <math>1.</math>
* Every [[locally compact group]] has a [[Haar measure]] that is invariant under the group action ([[translation (group theory)|translation]]).
